extracted.intended_audience: designers, journalists, educators, marketers, and general readers interested in creating or evaluating infographics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and assessing infographics and data visualizations, covering design principles, visualization types, communication goals, and medium/tool considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tufte's graphical display principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical displays should: show the data; induce the viewer to think about the substance rather than about methodology, graphic design, the technology of graphic production, or something else; avoid distorting what the data has to say; present many numbers in a small space; make large data sets coherent; encourage the eye to compare different pieces of data; reveal the data at several levels of detail, from a broad overview to the fine structure; serve a reasonably clear purpose: description, exploration, tabulation, or decoration; be closely integrated with the statistical and verbal descriptions of a data set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these principles as a checklist: prioritize accurate, non-distorting presentation; compactly present many numbers while enabling comparison and multi-level inspection; tie graphics closely to accompanying statistical/verbal descriptions. The article emphasizes 'Graphics reveal data' and that graphics can be more precise and revealing than conventional statistical computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of an infographic (visual, content, knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics consist of three parts: the visual (colors and graphics; theme and reference graphics), the content (statistics and facts from sources like census data and news reports), and the knowledge (the insight into the data that the infographic provides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing/evaluating, ensure visuals support and do not obscure content; reference graphics (icons) can point to data but are optional; the infographic must provide some insight (knowledge) beyond raw facts. Verify sources for content and that the visual treatment communicates the intended insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six components of visual encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: The six components of visual encoding are spatial, marks, connection, enclosure, retinal properties, and temporal encoding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each encoding channel to represent relationships between data types. The page notes spatial position is the most effective for numerical data, so prioritize spatial encodings for key relationships. Use other encodings (color, shape, connection lines, enclosure) where appropriate to add dimensions or clarify structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three provisions of communication: appeal, comprehension, retention
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing an infographic, assess three communication provisions: 'appeal' (engage the audience), 'comprehension' (the viewer should be able to easily understand the information), and 'retention' (the viewer should remember the data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize these provisions according to purpose: for academic/scientific infographics prioritize comprehension > retention > appeal; for commercial infographics prioritize appeal > retention > comprehension; for editorial/newspaper purposes prioritize appeal > comprehension > retention. A comprehensible layout can often combine appeal and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'chartjunk' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over-decorate graphics to the point of losing the information contained within them — Edward Tufte coined the term 'chartjunk' for such decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decorations against whether they obscure or distract from the data. Remove or reduce purely decorative elements that interfere with accurate reading or comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate visualization by graphical features
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial to identify the appropriate visualization for the data set by taking into consideration graphical features such as position, size, shape, and color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by classifying the data/problem into one of the primary visualization categories (time-series, statistical distributions, maps, hierarchies, networking) then select encodings (position, size, color, shape) that best express the key relationships. The article stresses that many visualization types can represent the same data — choose the one that optimizes comprehension and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-series visualization considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-series visualizations document values over time; examples include index charts, stacked graphs, small multiples, and horizon graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use index charts when relative changes matter more than raw values (e.g., percentage change). Stacked graphs show aggregate and individual patterns but do not support negative numbers and can make trend interpretation difficult; consider small multiples as an alternative to show each series separately for clearer individual trends. Horizon graphs increase data density while preserving resolution — useful when space is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical distribution visualization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical distributions reveal trends in how numbers are distributed. Common examples include histograms and box-and-whisker plots which convey features like mean, median, and outliers. Alternatives include stem-and-leaf plots, Q–Q plots, scatter plot matrices (SPLOM), and parallel coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the chart based on the analytic focus: use histograms/boxplots for single-variable distribution and outlier detection; stem-and-leaf for frequency-focused inspection; Q–Q plots to compare distributions; SPLOM for pairwise relations across variables; parallel coordinates to compactly show many variables (note tradeoffs in interpretability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Map/geovisualization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps naturally represent geographical data; techniques include flow maps for time/space, choropleth maps (encode data through color by region), graduated symbol maps (use symbols sized by value), and cartograms (distort region shapes to encode a variable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose map type according to the data and message: use choropleths for density/ratio measures across regions, graduated symbols if you need symbol-based magnitude comparisons, and cartograms to directly encode a variable by area. Be mindful of geographic misinterpretation when distorting shape or using inappropriate color scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy visualization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchical data can be organized using node-link diagrams, adjacency diagrams, and enclosure diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use node-link diagrams for tidy, tree-like representations where branching is important; adjacency diagrams (space-filling) when representing size proportion within hierarchy is important; enclosure diagrams (containment) to show grouping relationships. Choose the layout that best communicates both structure and size relationships while preserving readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network visualization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Network visualization explores relationships such as friendships and cliques; common types include force-directed layouts, arc diagrams, and matrix views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force-directed layouts are intuitive for small-to-moderate networks; arc diagrams are useful as one-dimensional layouts to reveal cliques and bridges (with good node ordering); matrix views scale well for large, dense networks because they avoid line crossings and can encode link values via color/saturation but make path-following difficult. Select layout based on network size, density, and the analytic tasks (e.g., path finding vs cluster identification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple visualization types and narrative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many modern infographics combine multiple visualization types in one graphic along with illustrations and text; some infographics do not contain actual data and instead present colorful, succinct ways to convey knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining types, ensure consistent encoding and that added illustrations/text support rather than obscure the data. Be aware that a sizeable portion of popular infographics may prioritize narrative/visual appeal over raw data — evaluate whether that tradeoff is appropriate for the infographic's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for mass communication (accessibility/simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics for mass communication are designed with fewer assumptions about the readers' knowledge base than other visualizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, simple explanations, and intuitive legends/labels when the target audience is broad. Avoid jargon and complex encodings that assume specialist knowledge; ensure the main insight can be grasped quickly (important in social media contexts and short attention-span environments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate tools and media for production
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics can be created by hand or with computer software (vector/raster, HTML5/CSS3, desktop publishing, GIS); templates and collaborative online tools can speed production and allow real-time collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tools that support the intended output medium (print, web, interactive). Prefer vector graphics for scalability, use interactive web technologies (HTML5/CSS3) for dynamic/interactive infographics, and choose templates or collaboration platforms to streamline workflow. Ensure technical choices do not compromise readability or data fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess cognitive load and layout effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Layout affects comprehension; studies (including neural network-based cognitive load estimation) have examined how infographic layouts influence viewer comprehension and cognitive load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate layouts for cognitive load: prefer layouts that lead the eye through the information, reduce unnecessary visual complexity, and structure information to support the intended comprehension/retention goals. Test or estimate cognitive load when designing complex infographics, especially for instructional or academic purposes.
